1251.event_title: Rumi meets Shams of Tabriz in Konya
1251.event: Jalal al-Din Rumi, a scholar and teacher who had taken over his father's post in Konya, met the wandering Sufi Shams of Tabriz around 1244, and the two became close companions. The friendship strained Rumi's relations with his students, family and associates, and Shams later left the city and was never seen again, around 1248. After this Rumi turned to mystical poetry, music and dance, and his major works, including the collection of lyrics named after Shams, date from this period.
1251.explanation: A respected and self-contained scholar was so overcome by a single bond of love that his settled life and reputation gave way, and the feeling poured out in poetry.
1251.tie_back: The kural says the axe of love smashes the door of reserve; Rumi's scholarly composure was broken open by his love for Shams in just this way.
1251._accuracy_note: Next-best: the overpowering of a reserved, respected man by love fits the image, but the love is spiritual friendship rather than the separated wife's romantic longing the kural describes.

1252.event_title: Pliny the Younger writes to Calpurnia of his sleepless nights
1252.event: In a short letter to his wife Calpurnia, who was away from him, the Roman senator and author Pliny the Younger wrote that he missed her badly, partly from love and partly because they were not used to being apart. He told her that he lay awake much of the night thinking of her, and that at the hours when he used to visit her, his feet carried him to her room, where he turned away sad from the empty doorway. He said he found relief only in the hard work of pleading cases in court.
1252.explanation: The letter is one of the best-known personal records from ancient Rome of a husband's longing during a separation, and scholars note how it borrows the language of Latin love poetry.
1252.tie_back: The kural says pitiless love keeps working on the heart even at midnight while others rest; Pliny describes exactly this, lying awake at night and drawn by longing to an empty room.
1252._accuracy_note: Strong fit: night-time sleeplessness ruled by love is the heart of both, though the speaker is a husband rather than the waiting wife.

1253.event_title: Elizabeth Barrett's Sonnets from the Portuguese
1253.event: Elizabeth Barrett wrote a sequence of 44 love sonnets during her courtship with the poet Robert Browning, whom she met in 1845. She kept them as a private record and gave them to him only after their secret marriage and move to Italy in 1846. When they were published in her Poems of 1850, she titled them Sonnets from the Portuguese, a disguise that made them look like translations and hid how personal they were.
1253.explanation: Barrett tried to keep her love private and then to veil it with a misleading title, yet the feeling in the poems made them some of the most famous love poems in English.
1253.tie_back: The kural's heroine would hide her love but it bursts out like a sneeze; Barrett's love, written in secret and then disguised, still came out for all to read.
1253._accuracy_note: Reasonable: concealed love that nonetheless shows itself matches, but Barrett chose to publish, so the outburst was not involuntary as in the sneeze image.

1254.event_title: The Bamangwato kgotla debates Seretse Khama's marriage
1254.event: Seretse Khama, heir to the chieftaincy of the Bamangwato people, married Ruth Williams, an Englishwoman, in a London registry office in September 1948, against the wishes of his uncle and regent Tshekedi Khama. The marriage was then debated at three meetings of the kgotla, the people's public assembly; at the December 1948 meeting most of those present opposed it. At the third kgotla, in June 1949, the assembly changed its position and accepted Seretse as chief and Ruth as his wife.
1254.explanation: A private marriage became a matter for open debate in the community's assembly and later for the British government, showing how personal love can become public business.
1254.tie_back: The kural's heroine says her love has left concealment and now shows itself in the maṉṟu, the public assembly; Seretse's love was literally argued over in the kgotla.
1254._accuracy_note: Reasonable to strong: love openly exposed in a public assembly matches closely, though Seretse never claimed to be hiding his love, and the kural's speaker is a woman losing her reserve.

1255.event_title: Berlioz pursues Harriet Smithson, who does not answer
1255.event: In 1827 the young composer Hector Berlioz fell in love with the Irish-born actress Harriet Smithson after seeing her play Ophelia with an English theatre company in Paris. They had not met, and she left his many passionate letters unanswered for a long time. His obsession inspired the Symphonie fantastique, first performed on 5 December 1830; Smithson heard a revised version in 1832, the two were introduced soon after, and they married in October 1833.
1255.explanation: Berlioz kept pursuing a woman who showed no interest in him, turning his unreturned feeling into one of the most famous symphonies of the Romantic era.
1255.tie_back: The kural says those sick with love do not know the dignity of refusing to follow someone who has turned away; Berlioz, unanswered, kept writing and kept pursuing.
1255._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of love overriding pride in pursuing someone unresponsive; the kural's person, however, is a wife pursuing an absent husband, not a stranger.

1256.event_title: Charlotte Bronte's letters to Constantin Heger
1256.event: After returning home from Brussels in 1844, Charlotte Bronte wrote a series of letters to Constantin Heger, her former teacher there. He replied rarely and, by the end of 1845, had stopped answering, while her letters grew more desperate; four survive, the last dated 18 November 1845. The letters were torn up at some point and later mended, and Heger's children gave them to the British Museum in 1913; they are now in the British Library.
1256.explanation: The letters show a proud and private writer unable to stop reaching out to someone who had withdrawn from her.
1256.tie_back: The kural's heroine marvels at a strange grief that makes her long to follow the one who has turned away; Bronte's letters to a silent Heger are a documented case of just such longing.
1256._accuracy_note: Strong fit for longing that pursues someone who has turned away, though Heger was a teacher she loved without return, not a husband who had left.

1257.event_title: Queen Victoria's journal on her wedding day
1257.event: Queen Victoria married Prince Albert on 10 February 1840. That night she wrote in her journal about Albert's great love and affection, calling him her precious Angel and saying his love gave her a happiness she had never hoped to feel. She ended the entry by calling it the happiest day of her life.
1257.explanation: A reigning monarch, trained to be reserved in public, wrote with complete openness once her husband showed her love.
1257.tie_back: The kural says that when the beloved, out of love, does what one longs for, shyness is forgotten; Victoria's unguarded wedding-night journal shows reserve melting in the warmth of returned love.
1257._accuracy_note: Next-best: the journal shows reserve giving way to openness in returned love, but it is a private diary, not a scene of shyness forgotten in the beloved's presence.

1258.event_title: Pierre Curie's letters persuade Marie Sklodowska to return to Paris
1258.event: Marie Sklodowska met the physicist Pierre Curie in Paris in the spring of 1894. Her plan had always been to return to Poland and teach, and in the summer of 1894 she went home unsure whether she would come back; she later wrote that marriage would have meant abandoning her country and family. Pierre's heartfelt letters helped persuade her to return to Paris and work alongside him, and they married in a simple civil ceremony at Sceaux on 25 July 1895.
1258.explanation: Marie's firm plan to return home gave way before Pierre's patient, persuasive words, beginning one of the most famous partnerships in science.
1258.tie_back: The kural's heroine says her beloved's gentle, coaxing words were the army that broke down her firmness; Pierre's letters did the same to Marie's resolve to leave France.
1258._accuracy_note: Strong: gentle persuasive words overcoming a woman's firm resolve match closely; the kural's playful 'thief' tone is absent.

1259.event_title: Abraham Lincoln and Mary Todd reconcile and marry
1259.event: Abraham Lincoln and Mary Todd, engaged in Springfield, broke off their courtship on 1 January 1841, a day Lincoln later called the fatal first of January; Mary's sister and brother-in-law disapproved of the match. After more than a year apart, friends brought them together again and they resumed their courtship in secret. They married on 4 November 1842 at her sister's house, and Mary told her sister they were courting again only on the wedding day.
1259.explanation: A couple who had separated in hurt found, when brought together again, that their attachment was stronger than their resolve to stay apart.
1259.tie_back: The kural's heroine set out to sulk but embraced her husband when she saw her heart already running to him; Lincoln and Mary Todd likewise gave up their separation once they met again.
1259._accuracy_note: Next-best: separation followed by reunion fits the shape, but this was a broken engagement lasting over a year, not a brief lovers' sulk.

1260.event_title: Charles Darwin weighs marriage on paper, then proposes
1260.event: In 1838 Charles Darwin wrote two notes weighing the case for and against marriage, listing companionship, a home and children against lost time, money and freedom. The second note, probably written in July 1838, came down on the side of marrying. On 11 November 1838 he proposed to his cousin Emma Wedgwood, who accepted, and they married on 29 January 1839; the notes are kept at Cambridge University Library.
1260.explanation: Even one of history's most methodical minds could not keep his feelings in the cool columns of a list; the case for love won.
1260.tie_back: The kural asks whether hearts that melt like fat in fire can ever hold firm; Darwin's careful balance sheet tipped toward marriage, showing calculation giving way to feeling.
1260._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shows reasoned restraint yielding to love, but there is no sulk or quarrel with a beloved as in the kural.
